newsitem.title: UK: Yugoslavia flexible on debt instruments - Djunic.
newsitem.headline: Yugoslavia flexible on debt instruments - Djunic.

text.p: A top Yugoslav debt negotiator said on Wednesday that his country could negotiate the method of restructuring its $2.4 billion commercial debt, but its current proposal -- which seeks 80 percent forgiveness -- was the best it could offer.
"We are flexible as to the instruments the bankers propose. We did not say take it or leave it and we are ready to do what is best for the markets," deputy prime minister Danko Djunic said.
"We are not insisting on a syndicated loan and are ready to go for bonds," he told a news conference at the Yugoslav Embassy.
Djunic led the Yugoslav delegation at two days of inconclusive negotiations with the London Club of bank creditors, which ended on Tuesday.

According to the proposal, obtained by Reuters, Yugoslavia wants 80 percent forgiveness of its outstanding commercial bank debt, both on interest and principal, with the issue of $481 million via a syndicated loan with a 25-year maturity and a nine-year grace period.

Yugoslavia, whose economy has been wrecked by Western sanctions imposed for Belgrade's role in the Bosnian war, owes around $10 billion in total. Economists also say the country has been slow to implement market reforms following the end of communism.

Djunic said bankers regarded the current proposal as aggressive but it was the best Belgrade could offer. "We are ready to sacrifice as much as we can, but we cannot stretch too far and then not deliver or even default on the bond issue," he said.
"Everyone is bothered about the 80 percent. It is a red flag, but we cannot repay more as we have to repay the IMF, the World Bank and the Paris Club as well."
The Paris club is a forum of Western governments which handles renegotiation of state-guaranteed debt.
A banking source close to the London club talks dismissed the Yugoslav proposal on Tuesday as "not a basis for any negotiation".

International Monetary Fund (IMF) membership is not a precondition for Yugoslavia to restructure its debt but analysts said a standby loan would have to be arranged as part of any debt repayment deal with creditors.

Djunic declined to say when Yugoslavia could join the IMF but said he hoped it could be by the year-end. "It is a dream that we will be a member by the end of the year. We want to play by the rules of the IMF and the World Bank," he told Reuters.
He said previous presentations on the country's economy had been "unrealistically optimistic". "There is a sense of reality in our (current) approach and our ability to pay," he said.
Djunic has offered to host the next round of talks of the bankers led by Chase Manhattan in Belgrade in July.
"If you don't think you will win the race you enter then you will never win," he said. "We have to start somewhere, I am looking forward to reaching an agreement."
